text: Good evening. I would like to call the regular meeting of May 26, 2026 to order. Welcome everyone to our chamber. I would like to invite Junior Troop 50228 to lead us in the Pledge of Allegiance. So if you are able and so choose, please rise for the Pledge of Allegiance.
I pledge allegiance to the flag of the United States of America and to the republic for which it stands, one nation, under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.

Thank you so much, ladies, and you are welcome to take a seat and stay for as much of our meeting as you would like to stay for. Now I'm going to ask Reverend Emma Chatton of the Metropolitan Church of Northern Virginia and friends to come down for the proclamation acknowledging June is LGBTQIA Pride Month.
Come on, everybody, just all over here. Come on, circle around, circle around, circle around. Gather, gather, gather. All right.

I love this proclamation every year. Whereas, within the recorded history of humanity, there have existed people around the world who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and intersex, living in cultures and communities that have shunned, shamed, ostracized, and criminalized their very existence.

a practice that continues in many places to this day. And whereas the contributions of those in the LGBTQ community have lifted our human experience through their art, innovation, discoveries, explorations, and in a variety of professions for centuries while being denied the basic human rights of others in their local communities.

And whereas the Stonewall Riots began in New York City on June 28, 1969 and are regarded as the catalyst for the gay liberation movement in the United States, bringing about a public display of pride and a celebration of people who refuse to cede their basic human rights to those who rigorously pursue a denial of those rights through dogma, antiquated beliefs, and discriminatory public policy.

And whereas in October 2014, same-sex couples were allowed to marry in the Commonwealth of Virginia as a result of long-term efforts by many advocates, and in advance of the U.S. Supreme Court ruling on June 25, 2015, that ended marriage discrimination for everyone in the United States of America.

And whereas in 2020, the Virginia General Assembly passed 13 pieces of civil rights legislation known as the Virginia Values Act that protect the LGBTQ community from discrimination in public employment, housing, credit, and public accommodation.

And whereas assaults on the rights of the LGBTQ individuals continue in legislative bodies across the country and around the world, necessitating constant vigilance and a resolve to protect the basic civil rights, human rights, and safety of our friends, neighbors, and loved ones.

And whereas the city of Fairfax wishes to recognize, celebrate, and uplift our LGBTQ residents and their allies with a celebration at the Stacey C. Sherwood Center on June 6th in collaboration with our partners at George Mason University, now therefore I, Catherine S. Reed, mayor of the city of Fairfax, on behalf of all residents of the city of Fairfax, do hereby proclaim June 2026 as LGBTQIA plus pride month in the city of Fairfax.

City of Fairfax, and urge all to acknowledge and celebrate our LGBTQIA plus friends, family, neighbors, employees, educators, and visitors to our welcoming and inclusive community. And with that, I will turn it over to Reverend Emily Chatton.

Fairfax is the best place to live. I will tell you that. I've lived in many places. I wouldn't imagine living any other place. I love it. I love the people. I love the places. I love everything about it.

I will tell you this much. People ask me what pride is. Our communities have a lot to be proud of. And the celebration of pride is just that. It's a part of an ongoing conversation with the world in which we live. Pride remembers our origins, our fights for our lives, our fights for our jobs, our fights to love, and our fights to be married, to be known as people, and to be known as human beings.

Pride is also a reminder that we need to draw from each other strength for tomorrow. That we need to draw strength from community and our history for our future and for the days ahead. In the year 2000, Fairfax County public schools did not have protections, explicit protections for gay and lesbian teachers.

And I remember going to countless school board meetings for that. And I remember Robert Rigby, who was a lion of the podium, in terms of making changes for that. Pride is about remembering that, because we've come too far to give up who we are, and that's what pride is about.
